references.text: John's prologue emphasizes that the new birth is not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (Joh 1:13). This clarifies that the birth Jesus speaks of is not a physical rebirth as Nicodemus misunderstood it.

Jesus says that "it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing" (Joh 6:63). This highlights the contrast between spiritual and physical, which Nicodemus fails to grasp when he thinks of a literal new birth.
Job raises a similar question about human limitation: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" (Job 14:1-4). This touches on the same theme of humanity's inability to renew itself.

When God asked Ezekiel if dry bones could live again, the prophet answered, "Lord GOD, you know" (Esek 37:3). The question of what is possible for humans points to the supernatural – just as Nicodemus' question about how a new birth is possible does.

God's promise to give a new heart and a new spirit (Esek 36:25-27) is the Old Testament background for the new birth. As Israel's teacher, Nicodemus should have known this promise and understood that regeneration is God's work, not a physical repetition.

Peter writes that believers are born again "not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God" (1 Pet 1:23). This confirms that the new birth is spiritual, not physical – in contrast to Nicodemus' literal understanding.

Paul emphasizes that God saved us "by the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit" (Tit 3:5). Regeneration is the work of the Spirit, which answers Nicodemus' wonder about how a new birth is possible.

John writes that whoever is born of God does not sin, for "God's seed remains in him" (1 Joh 3:9). The new birth is an inner, spiritual transformation – not a physical return to the womb, as Nicodemus imagined.

Paul writes: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, all things have become new" (2 Kor 5:17). This radical renewal is spiritual, not physical – a new creation, not a new physical birth as Nicodemus thought.

James writes: "Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth" (Jak 1:18). The new birth happens through God's word and will, which clarifies that Nicodemus' idea of a physical rebirth was a misunderstanding.
